# **Harmonizing Repeated Cross-Sectional Surveys for Pooled Longitudinal Analysis: Methodological Standards, Activity Crosswalks, and Mode-Adjustment Strategies**

## **Conceptual and Metadata Frameworks for Ex-Post Survey Harmonization**

Analyzing long-term social change and behavioral trends requires data spanning substantial temporal horizons.1 While prospective panel designs represent the gold standard for tracking individual-level transitions, they frequently suffer from compounding attrition, high operational costs, and panel conditioning.1 Consequently, researchers and statistical agencies rely heavily on repeated cross-sectional (RCS) surveys.1 Pooling multiple cross-sectional waves offers a mathematically rigorous alternative, facilitating the estimation of aggregate population-level shifts, cohort replacement dynamics, and historical trends.1  
Establishing historical and conceptual equivalence remains the primary challenge of pooling legacy RCS surveys.6 In survey methodology, harmonization strategies are divided into ex-ante (prospective) and ex-post (retrospective) designs.6 Ex-ante input harmonization occurs during the initial design phase of a multi-wave or cross-national survey project, enforcing uniform sampling frames, standardized questionnaires, and identical data collection protocols.6 Conversely, ex-post output harmonization operates on pre-existing microdata collections that were compiled independently and without an a priori coordination framework.6 Ex-post harmonization converts disparate source variables into standard, unified target variables.8  
Large-scale data infrastructures, such as the Consortium of European Social Science Data Archives (CESSDA), the Integrated Public Use Microdata Series (IPUMS), and the Data Documentation Initiative (DDI), provide standardized frameworks to govern ex-post harmonization workflows.10 These organizations emphasize that harmonization must not merely standardize variable names; it must rigorously document and align the underlying metadata, including survey universes, question wording, missing-value schemes, and administrative boundaries.13 Implementing these standards ensures that the pooled data satisfy the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) principles.20  
Advanced ex-post frameworks have introduced more systematic paradigms to standard social science research. The Survey Data Recycling (SDR) framework, pioneered by Slomczynski, Tomescu-Dubrow, and colleagues, integrates source data quality control directly into the ex-post harmonization process.22 SDR constructs two types of metadata: measures of source data quality (e.g., adequacy of survey documentation, sampling representative, frequency of processing errors) and control indicators for ex-post harmonization (e.g., mapping differences in question wording or response scale formal properties).22

| Dimension | Ex-Ante Input Harmonization | Ex-Post Output Harmonization |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Operational Stage** | Prior to data collection 6 | Post data collection and public dissemination 6 |
| **Control Over Process** | Centralized coordination of instruments 10 | Decentralized; managed retrospectively by secondary users 6 |
| **Primary Mechanism** | Uniform protocols, standardized sampling, standard questionnaires 10 | Structural mapping, category crosswalks, translation tables 12 |
| **Data Loss Risk** | Low; optimized for conceptual equivalence 10 | High; limited to the lowest common denominator 14 |
| **Key Metadata Standards** | DDI-Lifecycle, SDMX 17 | Translation tables, DDI-Codebook, SDR quality flags 13 |

New computational techniques are emerging to aid this process. For instance, the Harmony tool developed under the Infra4NextGen project utilizes Natural Language Processing (NLP) to automate the identification of conceptually similar survey items across diverse sources.27 Heizmann (2025) emphasizes that ex-post harmonization often requires resolving scale differences and structural breaks when instruments are revised over time.28 Techniques such as observed score equating in a random groups design (OSE-RG) represent advanced alternatives to simple linear stretching.7 OSE-RG transforms response scales based on empirical cumulative response distributions, aligning both numerical formats and the underlying "difficulty" of endorsing specific options.7

## **Activity-Classification Harmonization across Time-Use Survey Generations**

Time-use research represents a highly specialized domain of survey research.29 Unlike traditional stylized questionnaires that ask respondents to estimate time allocations, time-use survey (TUS) designs typically rely on 24-hour time-diary instruments.31 These instruments require respondents to record sequential primary and secondary activities, spatial locations, and social contexts in discrete intervals (e.g., 10-minute slots).31 Over multi-decade spans, the classifications used to code these raw descriptions inevitably undergo generational shifts.2  
The two main regional and global standards for time-use coding are the Harmonised European Time Use Surveys (HETUS) Activity Coding List (ACL) and the United Nations' International Classification of Activities for Time Use Statistics (ICATUS).31 ICATUS 2016 establishes a three-level hierarchical classification (comprising 9 major divisions, 56 divisions, and groups) designed to measure productive and personal (non-productive) activities comprehensively.34 HETUS has similarly updated its ACL, introducing categories like "ICT use" in Round 3 (2020) to capture digital engagement during 10-minute slots.31  
Pooling raw, uncrosswalked activity codes across different survey waves introduces severe methodological artifacts.13 Over time, raw codes experience semantic drift (where the same code refers to a different activity in subsequent waves) or structural splits (where a single historical category is disaggregated).13 For instance, "online shopping" might be subsumed under general computer use in early iterations, but coded as retail purchasing in later cycles.31  
To resolve these discrepancies, databases like the Multinational Time Use Study (MTUS) and IPUMS Time Use employ composite, hierarchical coding.14 The first one or two digits represent broad categories comparable across all cycles, whereas trailing digits capture detailed information available in only a subset of samples.13 Enforcing a common missing-value convention is also critical, distinguishing between structural missingness (e.g., skipping child care questions for childless households) and item non-response.19  
Practical applications of activity harmonization often require expert consensus. For instance, sleep, sedentary behavior (SB), light physical activity (LPA), and moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) cannot be directly extracted from standard ICATUS categories.41 Researchers have successfully utilized the Delphi consensus process to match and classify 542 distinct activities from Trial ICATUS 2005 and ICATUS 2016 into health-relevant physical intensity categories.41

## **Mode Effects on Time-Use and Behavioral Reporting**

A major challenge in pooling repeated cross-sections is the transition of data collection modes over time, most notably from interviewer-administered computer-assisted telephone interviewing (CATI) to self-administered computer-assisted web interviewing (CAWI).45 Mode changes introduce a combination of selection effects and measurement effects.46 Selection effects represent systematic demographic and socioeconomic differences in who chooses to respond across modes.45 For instance, highly educated, younger, and digitally literate individuals are significantly more likely to select CAWI.49 This is confirmed by the transition into adulthood supplement (TAS-2019) of the US Panel Study of Income Dynamics, where access to internet resources and high time-demands (e.g., from employment or schooling) strongly predicted web completion.50  
Measurement effects represent systematic differences in how respondents report their behaviors due to the intrinsic features of the administration mode.45 These are driven by several cognitive and contextual mechanisms:

* **Social Desirability Bias:** The presence of an interviewer in CATI triggers social norms, prompting respondents to overreport socially approved activities (such as active child care, exercising, or reading) and underreport stigmatized behaviors (such as drinking, sedentary passive leisure, or poor dietary practices).45  
* **Satisficing and Cognitive Effort:** While web self-administration provides a visual channel and a higher sense of privacy 45, the lack of an interviewer to motivate the respondent can lead to satisficing.45 Web respondents may complete diaries with minimal cognitive effort, resulting in shorter free-text descriptions and underreported secondary activities.29  
* **Primacy and Recency Effects:** The communication channel (visual vs. aural) influences response selection.45 CAWI questionnaires visually presenting response lists tend to induce primacy effects (selecting early options) 45, whereas CATI interviews reading options aurally are more susceptible to recency effects (selecting the last options heard).45  
* **Interviewer Probing:** In CATI, trained interviewers can probe vague entries, ensuring a complete 24-hour log and reducing skipped questions.30 This was illustrated in the CoVerlauf concurrent mixed-mode study, where CATI resulted in longer completion times but significantly fewer skipped responses compared to web self-completion.49

The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) and NORC tested these exact mode effects while developing a self-administered web diary tool for the American Time Use Survey (ATUS).32 Within-subject tests and pilot comparisons against CATI phone interviews revealed distinct mode measurement effects, highlighting the ongoing challenge of transitioning time-diary protocols from phone to web without compromising longitudinal trends.32 Similarly, South Korea's Patient Experience Assessment (PXA) parallel-group randomized controlled trial showed that mobile web surveys yielded significantly lower scores than telephone surveys across multiple subdomains, proving that the mode effect remains a robust systematic driver of measurement error.55

| Dimension | Computer-Assisted Telephone Interviewing (CATI) | Computer-Assisted Web Interviewing (CAWI) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Administration Type** | Interviewer-administered (high-touch) 45 | Self-administered (low-touch) 45 |
| **Stimulus Channel** | Aural (spoken interaction) 45 | Visual (screen presentation) 45 |
| **Cognitive Bias Bias** | Recency effects 45 | Primacy effects 45 |
| **Social Desirability** | High (interviewer triggers conformity) 45 | Low (increased privacy and anonymity) 45 |
| **Data Completeness** | High (fewer skipped entries due to probing) 30 | Variable (higher missingness/shorter text) 29 |

While computationally simple, this linear OLS approach does not easily generalize to bounded, binary, or ordinal categorical outcomes.58

### **Multiple Imputation (MI) Adjustment**

The mode effect is conceptualized as a missing data problem.58 For each respondent ![][image9], there exist potential outcomes under each mode, ![][image10] (response under CATI) and ![][image11] (response under web).58 Because we only observe the response in the completed mode, the counterfactual response is missing.55 Chained equations (MICE) are used to impute the unobserved counterfactual responses for the alternative mode, conditioned on the observed demographics and substantive variables.58

## **Longitudinal Comparability and Measurement Break Artifacts over Long Spans**

RCS surveys spanning multiple decades are highly vulnerable to contextual, systemic, and conceptual shifts.1 Tom Smith’s First Law of Societal Change warns that "the way to measure change is not to change the measure".2 Yet, in practice, long-term repeated surveys rarely escape modification.2 A key challenge is the Age-Period-Cohort (APC) identification problem.2 Because Age, Period (survey year), and Cohort (birth year) are perfectly collinear (![][image30]), modeling their independent effects requires identifying restrictions or specialized cross-sectional structures.2  
Longitudinal pooling also introduces measurement-regime structural breaks.7 A prominent example is the income-measurement regime change (e.g., shifting from continuous dollar reporting to discrete income brackets, or changing from gross earnings to net disposable income definitions).7 Changes in monetary variables over time must also account for inflation.62 The IPUMS Adjust Monetary Values (AMV) tool utilizes centralized, dynamic conversion factors using the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) to standardize monetary metrics to a single reference year.62 Income definitions are highly complex; disposable household income comprises labor income, capital income, and private/public transfers, minus deductions like taxes and social security.63 Shifting the survey concept from gross to disposable income, or changing the aggregation level, changes the underlying income-distribution parameters, creating an artificial longitudinal trend if uncorrected.7

## **Methodological Boundary Conditions and Cautionary Findings**

While statistical adjustments like adding a mode covariate or an income-regime flag are common, they fail under several specific, critical conditions 46:

### **Collider-Stratification Bias**

Georgia Tomova and colleagues (2025, 2026\) show that when mode selection is driven by individual characteristics, treating the mode as a covariate can introduce collider bias.47 If an unobserved factor like Socioeconomic Position (![][image31]) is a common cause of both survey mode completed (![][image3]) and the target outcome (e.g., healthy diet, ![][image32]), and another factor like Depression (![][image33]) also causes mode completion and diet reporting, then mode completed (![][image3]) acts as a *collider* on the path ![][image34].47 Simply conditioning on ![][image3] in a regression model opens this backdoor path, producing a spurious, biased association between Depression and Diet.47

### **Limitations of the MAR Assumption**

Post-hoc mode adjustments typically rely on the Missing at Random (MAR) assumption.55 However, South Korea's PXA trial demonstrated that late responders and non-responders systematically report less favorable outcomes, violating MAR.56 If the missingness is Missing Not at Random (MNAR), standard regression and multiple imputation adjustments remain biased.55 Sensitivity analyses using delta-adjustments under MNAR scenarios are required to test the robustness of the adjusted estimates.55

### **Treatment Effect Heterogeneity (TEH)**

Standard dummy variable adjustments assume that the mode effect is strictly additive and homogeneous across all demographic subgroups.66 However, if the mode effect interacts with covariates (e.g., if social desirability bias on alcohol reporting or childcare is stronger for certain genders or educational groups), a simple additive flag is highly misspecified.66 This misspecification masks substantial subgroup differences, biasing the estimated demographic effects.66 Algorithmic machine learning approaches (e.g., causal forests, SoftBART) are increasingly used to detect and model such high-dimensional treatment effect heterogeneities.66

## **Synthesized Analytical Framework**

The ex-post output harmonization of repeated cross-sectional surveys from 2005 to 2022 into a unified target schema provides a powerful framework for tracking longitudinal behavioral changes in time use.1 Rather than dropping compromised cycles, which severely reduces statistical power and truncates longitudinal trends, this study preserves all four cycles.6 This preservation is achieved by mapping raw inputs to a single target format: standardizing variable names, aligning missing-value conventions, and recoding category scales.12  
The critical core of this integration is the mapping of approximately 60+ raw activity codes to a standardized 14-category scheme.29 This mapping relies on the structural principles of ICATUS 2016 and HETUS, ensuring that productive, non-productive, and travel behaviors are partitioned into mutually exclusive and exhaustive target domains.34 To resolve structural inconsistencies, the analysis flags the data-collection mode transition (telephone CATI to self-administered web) and a major income-measurement regime change as explicit model covariates.46 This approach allows the statistical model to isolate and adjust for operational shifts mathematically, maintaining the continuity of the 17-year time series.60  
However, the application of post-hoc statistical corrections must be accompanied by rigorous diagnostic testing.47 Analysts must verify that the mode-adjustment covariates do not introduce collider-stratification bias, which occurs when unobserved factors jointly influence both mode selection and time-use outcomes.47 When the parallel-trends assumption is violated due to heterogeneous mode effects or structural changes in the income measurement regime, researchers must move beyond simple additive dummy models.7 Incorporating multiple imputation, econometric utility models, or non-linear score equating ensures that the longitudinal estimates represent true societal change rather than mere methodological artifacts.2
